scenario: A retail merchandiser uploads shelf photos and internal records and wants an audit.md report on packaging accuracy plus a competitor stock comparison.
did: The agent had to check each product's shelf packaging against internal records and compare stock quantities against three competitor products, writing both sections into audit.md.
why: All 12 criteria check out against the live conversation, the photos, and the source files, including the competitor stock-difference math. The only issue is C8, which is tagged as grading the agent's process when it actually grades the final report content like its sibling criteria C9 and C10, so the tag doesn't match what the criterion checks. That's a small labeling slip, not a real gap, and nothing else in the report goes unchecked, so this stays a light Non-Fail.
fix: Retag C8's evaluation target so it matches C9 and C10 (final content, not process).
agree: No — the second opinion flags it, but on a closer look the concern doesn't hold up.

scenario: A vlogger who just tried kayaking wants a polished thumbnail made from their standard photo, a draft text file, and photos of the trip while they're away editing the video.
did: The agent built the thumbnail with the requested overlay phrases, cropped out the mountains, and added a title with the distance and location, all based on what was actually in the draft file and photos.
why: Three checks (C6, C7, C8) demand an exact price, place name, and distance that never appear anywhere in the draft file or photos the agent was given, so the agent's faithful, accurate answer gets marked wrong. Two more checks (C4, C5) lock in one specific headcount and kayak count from photos that are genuinely hard to read precisely, and the agent's counts were reasonable reads of the same images. C2 also names the wrong file extension for the thumbnail, though that one didn't cost any points.
fix: Update C6, C7, and C8 to match the actual draft file (an unknown price, the real location, and the real distance) instead of unrelated made-up values. Loosen C4 and C5 to accept a small range of counts instead of one exact number, and fix the filename in C2 to the correct extension.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: Someone who slipped up on their meat-free challenge asks for a punishment/reward meal plan built from photos of their recent meals.
did: The agent had to look at six meal photos, count which ones had animal meat, and use that count to build a plan.md with the right number of weeks and the right number of meat-free meal slots.
why: C3 and C5 both lock in one specific reading of a photo that's genuinely ambiguous (a pasta dish with dark-red rounds that could reasonably be sun-dried tomato or could be chorizo). Only one of the two equally reasonable readings satisfies the exact day count and meat-free count these criteria demand, so a correct plan built on the other reasonable reading gets marked wrong.
fix: Loosen C3 and C5 so they accept either reasonable reading of the ambiguous photo (e.g. accept both the 1-week/10-of-14 and 2-week/8-of-28 outcomes), or clarify the intended reading with clearer visual evidence.
agree: Yes — both flag it as failing.

scenario: A gym-goer uploads photos of recent meals and asks for a plan tracking animal-meat variety.
did: The agent had to count distinct animal-meat sources per meal from the photos, sum and average them, and build a two-week protein-variety plan with energy data.
why: C2 locks the total meat-source count at exactly 6, but counting distinct meats in these photos is genuinely open to more than one reasonable reading (for example the pizza could defensibly be 2, 3, or 4 meats, the roast 1 or 2), and the agent's own reasonable count of 5 is rejected outright. C3, C4, and C5 all inherit that same fixed number to compute the average and the two weekly targets, so each one independently shuts out an equally valid answer. That's four criteria pinning one side of an ambiguous call, which is enough to fail.
fix: Loosen C2 (and the derived C3-C5) to accept a reasonable range of meat counts per meal instead of one exact total, or add tolerance to the average and weekly targets so a defensible alternate count still passes.
agree: No — I'm stricter here; the second opinion lets it pass.

That's a minor redundancy, not a wrong or missing check, so it doesn't bring the rubric down.
